articles.title: Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US
articles.summary: TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an…
body: The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security.

While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold.

articles.title: Why the robots are ditching Uber
articles.summary: In a late August earnings call, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi sounded optimistic about his company's "very strong" partnership with Waymo, the global leader in autonomous robotaxis.
body: Waymo and Serve Robotics are walking away from exclusive deals. Can Uber still be the default app for autonomy?
“We believe we’ll continue to operate next year in those marketplaces,” he gushed. “It’s a terrific product, and the on-the-ground partnership continues to be very strong.”

The partnership would turn out to be more brittle than Khosrowshahi let on. Several weeks later, Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana revealed in an interview that her company planned to end its exclusive robotaxi partnership with Uber, calling the mixed-fleet experience a “crapshoot” for its own customers. Starting in January 2028, riders in Austin and Atlanta will be able to use the Waymo app to hail driverless rides directly. The unlikely partnership, it would seem, was coming to an end.

Waymo isn’t alone in souring on its experience in the Uber ecosystem. Serve Robotics, which operates thousands of sidewalk delivery robots in dozens of US cities, recently announced it would not renew its partnership with Uber Eats when it expires in 2027.

articles.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
articles.summary: It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers. AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most.
body: Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.
The World Economic Forum finds analytical thinking is now the skill employers value most, and estimates that 59 in every 100 workers will need training to adapt to this shift by 2030.

In September, I found myself at the first Global Brain Economy Summit in New York asking a hard question: How much room is there for creativity and learning when one’s mind is consumed by anxieties about paying rent or for food to last through the week?
points: It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers.

articles.title: I’m a tech expert and new mum. Here’s what I learned testing 17 baby monitors
articles.summary: Our tech expert and new mum tested 17 monitors for picture quality, battery life and reliability – here’s what she recommends. • The best eco-friendly baby products. Moving my baby into her own room to sleep felt liberating and stressful.
body: There’s a huge range of baby monitors, from simple audio-only options to sophisticated video models. Some even include wearables or other devices to track a baby’s breathing or heart rate, while others offer AI features to analyse sleep patterns. At their most basic, baby monitors typically consist of a baby unit, which you position near the baby, and a parent unit, which lets you hear and/or see them. With video models, the baby unit is essentially a camera, while the parent unit is a screen. Many are also wifi-enabled, meaning you can connect the monitor to your smartphone and view the live feed through an app instead of using a dedicated parent unit (read on for security advice).

With so many types of baby monitors to choose from, it can be tricky to distinguish the useful features from those that are simply nice to have. To cut through the noise, I tested 17 different models to help you find the best baby monitor for your needs.

articles.title: The Smart Ring Goes to Church
articles.summary: From glowing crosses to voice-transcribed prayers, the Elah and Glorify rings are reimagining traditional faith rituals for the wearable era.
body: Stressed? Heart rate elevated? If you’re wearing a smart ring from Oura, Ultrahuman, or Samsung, the spike could prompt app suggestions like breathing exercises, meditations, or a physical reset like a short walk. So far, so Silicon Valley. But now you can add reading the Bible to that list of self-soothing activities.

The first generation of Christian smart rings is here, joining other religious wearables like iQibla’s dedicated Muslim smartwatches, rings, and Hajj bands alongside “kosher” smartwatch apps. Two new devices in particular—Glorify’s Ring and Everblessed Technology’s Elah Ring—connect to hugely popular Christian prayer apps with tens of millions of users, and both claim to be the world’s first Christian smart ring.

Both are first, in their own ways. Everblessed’s $249 Elah Ring S1 went on sale in October and is shipping in the US. The $299 Glorify Ring launched in July, with reservations open and shipping set for January 2027, but 77,000 units of an earlier beta iteration, the Amen Ring made by faith tech company ConfideIn (which merged with Glorify this May), were given away last Christmas. Everblessed manages the Blessed app, and Glorify has an eponymous app.
points: From glowing crosses to voice-transcribed prayers, the Elah and Glorify rings are reimagining traditional faith rituals for the wearable era.

articles.title: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
articles.summary: State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors. California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.
body: Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

articles.title: ‘We’re the most arrogant of all apes!’ A delightfully mind-expanding encounter with Peter Gabriel
articles.summary: From sampling to streaming, the rock legend has always been in thrall to technology – but is superintelligence a step too far? Back with an epic new album, he unpacks his remarkable ideas.
body: Peter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.”

articles.title: Muse Is Unleashing a World of Pettiness on Instagram
articles.summary: Meta’s AI assistant can track and unfollow Instagram users who don’t follow you back—and some people are taking full advantage.
body: Khalil Roberts had heard horror stories of people getting kicked off Instagram for using third-party apps to purge follower counts, so when he came across an X post claiming that Muse — Meta ’s AI assistant —could mass-unfollow people who didn’t follow him back, he didn’t believe it.

“I’ve never gone through my exact list to vet those people out, but I’ve always been curious,” the 31-year-old New Yorker tells WIRED. But after realizing that by using Muse, his account wouldn’t get flagged as spam, his mind was made up. “I was like, I actually will be a little petty.”

Within minutes, Muse identified 151 accounts. It attached an Excel sheet with a breakdown of everyone cataloged—separated by categories identifying their username, real name, classification, and profile link—and asked if Roberts wanted to proceed with his request. Shockingly, some of the names were people he thought of as friends. “It was a little surprising, but also a reminder that we don’t have a relationship anymore.”
points: Meta’s AI assistant can track and unfollow Instagram users who don’t follow you back—and some people are taking full advantage.

articles.title: Amazon fights the Delivery Protection Act with homepage banner, in-app pop-up
articles.summary: In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill. When I log into Amazon today, I’m met with a vertical banner that reads: “ATTENTION NYC Council could add up to $5 per order” with a button that says “Act now.” A…
body: I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website. The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn’t specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I’m logged into Amazon.

Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518 ), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses.

Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.
